## Methods

Tidal flat width and slope data
The width of the tidal flat is defined as the horizontal distance from mean high water to low water (Supplementary Fig. 15). The data of tidal flat area along China’s coastline were obtained based on the global tidal flat maps1. These maps used over 7.0×105 satellite images to record tidal flat extent, and the data explicitly exclude vegetation-dominated intertidal ecosystems (such as mangroves and vegetated marshes). The resultant global map of tidal flats exhibits a horizontal resolution of 30 m, delineating the spatiotemporal variation of tidal flats on a global scale. To obtain the width of China’s tidal flat, we measured the distance of cross-shore transects along the shoreline in OpenStreetMap (OSM)40 every 1 km. The overall accuracy of the tidal flat area map is 82.2%41. Misclassification of tidal flats (pixels) can occur in areas of highly turbid water, polluted areas, aquaculture ponds, and areas subject to strong wave action. Despite the potential errors, to our knowledge, this map is the only freely accessible tidal flat map that covers large spatial (national) and temporal (decadal) scales. The accuracy of this map is sufficient (>80%)41 to reveal the overall dynamics of tidal flat areas and to support the main findings of the current study.

The slope of the tidal flats was ascertained from the Foreshore Assessment using Space Technology (FAST) database21, which provides a high-resolution intertidal bathymetry/elevation dataset. The bed level data has a 20 m horizontal resolution and typically a 30-50 cm vertical accuracy. To obtain the tidal flat slope, we extracted the bed level data of cross-shore transects along the shoreline. The transect endpoints are based on the range of the tidal flats. The slope of the tidal flat was then calculated by the cross-shore horizontal length L of the transect and vertical height difference ΔH between the endpoints (i.e., slope=ΔH/L, Supplementary Fig. 16). Transects with discontinuous elevation were excluded from analysis (917 of 2538 transects). There are mainly two reasons that cause the discontinuous elevation: 1) gaps within the continuous elevation data (51.4%); 2) none or too few elevation data in the FAST database (48.6%).

To identify the key factors that sculpt the spatial morphology of tidal flats, we compared tidal flat width data (2014–2016) and slope data (1997–2017) with SSC (2016), tidal range (2010), and wave height (1979–2021). To reveal the temporal changes in tidal flat width, we traced the tidal flat width change data from 2002–2016 and SSC change data from 2003-2011, constrained by data availability. Changes in tidal flat width were obtained from tidal flats maps every three years (2002–2004, 2005–2007, 2008–2010, 2011–2013, and 2014–2016)1. The data on the annual variation in tidal flat width shows no significant spatial autocorrelation (Moran’s I < 0.01, p = 0.44).

Hydrodynamic data
We utilized the TPXO9-atlas dataset42 to obtain the mean tidal range for each cross-shore tidal flat transect along China’s coast. The spatial resolution of the dataset is 1/30°. The accuracy of the TPXO9 on China’s coast can be shown by an average Root Sum Squares (RSS) value of 19.92 cm43. Employing the tide model driver (TMD) tool, we processed the TPXO dataset to calculate the water levels at each transect for the year 2010. This was done by incorporating the amplitudes and phases of eight major tidal constituents: K1, K2, M2, N2, O1, P1, Q1, and S2. The average tidal range data was then interpolated from the mean high water level and the mean low water level.

Tidal asymmetry is calculated from the phase difference between the M2 and M4 tidal constituents (2θM2 − θM4). A phase difference within the range of 0–180° results in a flood-dominant tide. Conversely, a phase difference between 180° and 360° indicates an ebb-dominant tide44,45. Under the same phase difference, the amplitude ratio of M4 and M2 tidal constituents is used to indicate the magnitude of the tidal asymmetry. The tidal flats along China’s coastline exhibit a tidal range that varies from a minimum of 0.59 m near the Yellow River mouth to a maximum of 7.33 m on the southern Shandong Peninsula, with an average of 2.78 m.

We collected SLR data from 14 coastal sites in China46 and calculated the correlation between the SLR data and changes in local tidal flat width. However, the results indicate no significant correlation (p = 0.89). The annual mean sea level data of the 14 coastal sites are collected from the Permanent Service for Mean Sea Level47,48 (see Supplementary Table 1). To test the possible effect tidal range has on tidal flat width, we compared the tidal range change from the 12 UHSLC tide gauge sites49 with the tidal width changes. The results indicated no significant correlation between the tidal range changes and the nearby tidal flat width changes (p = 0.32), which is likely due to the relatively small changes in tidal range (averaged 1.1 cm per year).

The offshore wave conditions were derived from the ERA5 reanalysis database50, which encompasses comprehensive wave height and period data from 2002–2016. The database has been proven suitable for China’s coastal areas51, with data bias estimated at less than 0.1 m in deep waters. These data were firstly reprojected to align with the offshore positions of the tidal flat transects. Subsequently, the offshore wave height values were transferred to the wave height situated 3 km off the coast, equating to 78% of the offshore wave height52. In the absence of detailed nearshore bathymetry data, we assumed linear profiles from 3 km off the coast to the mean low water level53, while the intertidal bathymetry (low water to high water level) data are available from FAST21. The offshore depth is obtained from the ERA5 database. This approach allowed for the estimation of wave heights in the immediate vicinity of the tidal flats at mean low water level, accounting for wave shallowing and bottom friction54:

Dw = 3/2 π ρf e Uδ 3 (1)

Uδ = Ts / π in Hh s kh (2)

where Dw is the wave height dissipation, ρ is the water density, f e is the wave friction factor, which is assigned a value of 0.05555, Uδ is the wave orbital velocity, H s is the significant wave height, T is the wave period, k is the wave number, and h is the water depth. Wave refraction and diffraction processes are not accounted due to the lack of nearshore bathymetry data.

To assess if a change in waves might affect tidal flat width, we calculated the change rate of significant wave height at 105 sites along the coast of China (with a resolution of 0.5 degrees) from ERA5 data. It shows that 95% of tidal flat areas have experienced a minimal variation in significant wave height below 0.1 cm/year from 2002 to 2016. Thus, there is no significant correlation between the wave height change and tidal flat width dynamics (p = 0.42).

To validate the applicability of the ERA5 data, we collected wave data from tidal flats at various locations along China’s coast, including Chongming Island56,57 and Leizhou Bay58 for both wave height and period, Taiwan Longdong59 and the Yellow River mouth60 for wave height, and Jiangsu61 for wave period. The agreement between our estimated wave heights and periods with in-situ observations (Supplementary Tables 2 and 3) confirms good applicability of ERA5 wave data. In the current study, the impact of alongshore currents is not explicitly considered, since there is a lack of nationwide dataset on alongshore currents. Yet, as alongshore currents transport sediment over large scales62,63, their impact is implicitly reflected by the SSC data we analyzed.

Suspended sediment concentration (SSC) data
SSC is considered representative of the local sediment availability36–38,64, and a key external driver on tidal flat morphodynamics. The SSC data near the monitoring tidal flat transects were obtained from the GlobColour project (https://www.globcolour.info). The data product of total suspended matter concentration (TSM, mg/L) produced by the project is used to represent SSC (mg/L) because in turbid coastal waters most suspended matters are due to suspended sediments. It is estimated from satellite-derived particle back-scattering coefficient in the blue wavelength by assuming a back-scattering/scattering ratio of 0.015, and such a product has been previously used and found reliable for large scale analyzes64,65. The spatial patterns of such derived TSM are consistent with those from independent studies using other algorithms66. Although satellite-derived TSM (or SSC) represents the particle concentration in surface waters (down to an optical depth), for both well-mixed water column or highly stratified waters it can be used as a proxy for suspended particles in the water column66. This is because, for the former case it is obvious that TSM reflect the overall sediment concentration and, for the latter case, the signals from the bottom, particle-rich layer will only be attenuated slightly by the surface, particle-poor layer. The applicability of this approach has been validated in terms of both spatial distribution67 and temporal variability68, and the method has been widely applied in previous studies (e.g., sediment availability data in ref. 64 and turbidity for estuaries in ref. 69).

The SSC data product has a horizontal resolution of 1/24 degree (generally 2.2 km off the coast) and a temporal resolution of one month. To investigate the drivers behind the spatial distribution of tidal flat morphology, we analyzed the monthly average SSC data obtained through the inversion of OLCI satellite data for the year 2016, synchronized with the tidal flat width (2002 - 2016) and slope data (1997 - 2017). In the Hangzhou Bay area, the maximum SSC reaches up to 200 mg/L, which is in line with previous field observations70,71. To assign a local sediment concentration level to each tidal flat data point, the TSM data point close to the tidal flat is defined as the sediment availability for the tidal flat. We defined sediment-starved systems in China as the areas with an annual mean SSC below the national mean SSC level (50 mg/L). This value is obtained by calculating the average SSC of pixels containing tidal flats (4 km resolution). Correspondingly, areas with an annual average SSC higher than 75 mg/L are defined as sediment-rich systems, which are the annual mean SSC in 5 major estuaries (the Changjiang River estuary, the Yellow River estuary, the Pearl River estuary, the Minjiang River estuary, and the Liaohe River estuary). These thresholds can be considerably higher than other countries17,69, due to the overall higher SSC on China’s coast. Thus, sediment-starved and sediment-rich systems should be defined differently in other regions of the world.

Human impact through conversion
Conversion of tidal flats to other land use directly and indirectly influence the evolution of tidal flats. To investigate the morphological evolution of large-scale tidal flat systems with environmental factors (i.e., hydrodynamic forcing and sediment availability), we excluded transects affected by direct conversion. First, we identified tidal flat transects with direct conversion by analyzing satellite imagery (see Supplementary Fig. 12). The tidal flats are mainly converted to agriculture or aquaculture land use, and also (about 1.2%) to artificial sandy beaches in areas like Xiamen city72. 750 transects are affected by direct conversion, which are excluded from our analysis.

To compare the effects of direct conversion and external drivers, we identified nine transects that were converted at the beginning of our study period and have SSC change data, so that we can track their development. The results show that eight out of nine transects exhibited a seaward progradation trend after the conversion (Supplementary Fig. 11). The rate of tidal flat width change exceeds the rate of tidal flat evolution driven by natural drivers, highlighting the important difference imposed by direct conversion and the necessity to exclude those transects in our study.

As conversion can also affect nearby hydrodynamic conditions, thereby influencing adjacent remaining tidal flat evolution by far-field effects. Therefore, we further excluded transects adjacent to those directly impacted by conversion. We identified nine estuaries or bays where the conversion level is high (over 40% of the transects were directly converted), including Qinjiang Estuary, Yingzai River Estuary, Zhenhai Bay, Luojiang Estuary, Wenzhou Bay, Wulei Island Bay, Liaohe Estuary, the southern coast of Hangzhou Bay, and Qixing Reef. The remaining transects were identified as being influenced by far-field effects of conversion. Additionally, those adjacent to converted transects along the open coast are also deemed influenced by far-field effects. After excluding all these 156 transects, our primary conclusions regarding spatial and temporal patterns remain unchanged (See Supplementary Fig. 13).

Statistical analysis
Multiple Linear Models (MLM) were used to identify the key drivers that shape the spatial distribution of tidal flat morphology.

The statistical analysis were performed using the ‘R’ software. MLMs were created for tidal flat width and tidal flat slope, respectively. Given the low resolution of offshore wave height data (0.5°), we consolidated data points that corresponded to the same offshore wave height and computed the mean values for tidal flat width, significant wave height (Hs), suspended sediment concentration (SSC), and tidal range (TR) within each offshore wave height pixel.

First, we used stepwise linear regression to select the best combination of independent variables that explain the spatial distribution of the tidal flat morphology. This process was guided by the selection of the model yielding the lowest Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) scores, a widely accepted criterion for model selection73–75. For tidal flat width and slope, SSC and tidal range were included in the most streamlined final model. Subsequently, we established a multiple linear regression model for the selected variables (Eq. 3 and Eq. 4) and calculated their relative importance. The relative importance is calculated as the contribution to the model’s determination coefficient (R2).

width3 1(cid:3)SSC3 1+TR3 1 (3)

log(slope)(cid:3)SSC3 1+TR3 1 (4)

To obtain a normal distribution of the data for proper statistical analysis, we applied transformations to the tidal flat width, tidal range, and SSC data by taking their cube roots, and log-transformed the tidal flat slope data prior to their inclusion in the statistical models. Considering the potential impact of spatial autocorrelation, we calculated Moran’s I for the residuals in our regression models for width (0.35, p<0.01) and slope (0.11, p=0.17). We then used a spatial error model to eliminate the effects of spatial autocorrelation for the width model, achieving a better fit than the multiple linear regression (R2=0.61). P-values and R-squared values were calculated using the ‘summary’ function in the linear model, and the relative importance of each parameter was calculated using the ‘relaimpo’ package75.

DET-ESTMORF model
To explore the relationship between sediment availability variations and the corresponding temporal shifts in tidal flat width, we utilized a one-dimensional tidal flats morphological model, DET-ESTMORF (Fig. 4 and Fig. 5)11. This model is a hybrid approach that integrates morphological equilibrium20,22 with hydrodynamic and sediment transport processes, in contrast to fully process-based models12. This model has been validated previously11, and applied in intertidal biogeomorphology studies76.

Tidal flats in morphological equilibrium are characterized by a consistent distribution of bottom bed shear stress and SSC throughout their profile. When the actual local bed shear stress surpasses the equilibrium shear stress, there is a tendency of erosion, requiring a higher SSC to counteract the tendency and maintain equilibrium, i.e., a higher local equilibrium concentration than average. Hence, the magnitude of bottom bed shear stress determines the tendency of tidal flats’ geomorphic change, while the difference between actual SSC and local equilibrium SSC indicate the occurrence of geomorphic change, which is similar to the process-based models, e.g., Delft3D.

In DET-ESTMORF, we considered both the effects of wave and tidal shear stresses on the bottom bed. To obtain the tidal-induced bottom bed shear stress, we adapted the method based on mass conservation from a previous study55. Concerning the wave propagation modeling, we applied the wave energy flux conservation equation considering bottom friction54:

d/dx (Ec cg) = −Dw (5)

where E is the wave energy [kg m−2 s−2)], cg is the group velocity (s2 m−1), and g is the acceleration of gravity (ms−2). The incident H s is obtained by a random draw from the Rayleigh distribution around a given mean value54.

The attenuation of wave energy by friction is given by Eq. 1 and Eq. 2. We also considered the effect of wave breaking in the wave propagation process, where the maximum wave height H s is associated with the local water depth and the breaking height coefficient:

H s = min (H s, γ b h) (6)

where γ b is a constant value (0.5). The bed stress induced by waves τ w is quantified as77:

τ w = 1/4 ρfwUδ 2 (7)

where f w is a friction factor estimated as:

f w = 1.39 (Aδ / k b) −0.52 (8)

Where the wave orbital semi-excursion at the bed Aδ=UδT, bed roughness k b = 2πd 50 = 12, and d 50 is the median grain size of sediment particles. The mean bed shear stress under combined waves and tidal currents during a wave cycle is calculated as78

τ m = τ cur [1 + 1.2 (τ wave / (τ cur + τ wave)) 3.2] (9)

Thus, the maximum bed shear stress during a wave cycle is calculated as

τ max = (τ m 2 + τ wave 2 + 2(τ m τ wave) cosθ) 0.5 (10)

where θ is the angle between current direction and direction of wave propagation. In our study, θ = 0 as both currents and wave propagation are in the cross-shore direction. τ 90 is quantified every 30 minutes during a tidal cycle. Subsequently, τ 90 is derived as the 90th percentile of τ max over a tidal cycle, which is considered as the hydrodynamic forcing that drives morphological changes.

In morphological equilibrium, the balance between erosion and accretion in the vertical direction is achieved, which can be expressed as follows79,80:

τ m / τ cr − 1 = w s / c E (11)

Here, m represents the erosion coefficient [kg m−2 s−1)], τ cr denotes the critical shear stress (Pa), and w s represents the sedimentation rate (m/s), c E is the long-term average SSC value (mg/L) at the seaward boundary. Via this equation, τ E is the uniform bed shear stress (Pa) that can be derived from the known variables. Subsequently, the local equilibrium concentration c e based on the ratio of τ 90 to τ E can be derived as:

c e = c E (τ 90 / τ E) n (12)

The local equilibrium concentration c e can be converted to volume concentration by dividing the sediment density (ρ s = 2650 kg/m3)81. The actual spatial and temporal distributions of local SSC are obtained by solving the diffusion equation:

∂(hc) / ∂t = w s (c e − c) + ∂/∂x (D ∂c/∂x) (13)

where c is the volume sediment concentration (m3/m3), and D represents the diffusion coefficient (m2 s−1). The change in tidal flats morphology following each tidal cycle is calculated based on the difference between c and c e:

∂z / ∂t = 1 / (1 − p) w s (c − c e) (14)

where z is the bed elevation (m), and p is the bed porosity. The key parameters are detailed in supplementary Table 4, and the values of these parameters are based on previous modeling work (Supplementary Table 5)10,12,82.

To reveal the nonlinear response of tidal flat width to SSC change, we selected two sites for explanatory modeling, namely the Western Scheldt site in the Netherlands (sediment-starved)76 and Jiangsu in China (sediment-rich)63. We did not select a Chinese site for the case study of sediment-starved area, as it was not possible to find detailed field data for model validation in China, while the Western Scheldt has a unique detailed dataset available. At the Western Scheldt site (SSC=58 mg/L), the DET-ESTMORF model has been applied and validated in previous studies11,76. At the Jiangsu site, we obtained the equilibrium profile by performing a 100-year modeling from the initial linear profile based on the tide level, while wave height and offshore SSC data (134 mg/L) are based on the collected datasets in the current study. We validated the model’s accuracy by comparing the obtained equilibrium profile with the observed profile reported in a previous study (Supplementary Fig. 17)63. Building on this validation, we proceeded to calculate equilibrium profiles for both sites under varying interannual SSC change rates, including −1.2%, −0.8%, 0.8%, and 1.2%. This exercise was designed to ascertain the interannual rates of tidal flat width change over a 13-year period, in line with the observational time frame spanning from 2003 to 2015.

Analysis of temporal changes in tidal flats width
To analyze the temporal changes in tidal flat width, we integrated measured data (the bubble chart of Fig. 5a) with experimental results (colormap of Fig. 5a). We extracted tidal width change rate of tidal flats with SSC above 50 mg/L and those below 50 mg/L across different SSC change rate groups (−3% to −1.5%/year, −1.5% to 0%/year, 0% to 1.5%/year, 1.5% to 3%/year). Within each group, we chose median tidal width change (mean of the 48%–52% percentiles) as the representative value (Fig. 5a). To minimize the influence of anthropogenic factors on the geomorphology of tidal flats, data points exhibiting interannual tidal width trends exceeding 20% per year were omitted.

We then employed the DET-ESTMORF model to simulate the variation of tidal flat width under different SSC (20~120 mg/L) and varying interannual rates of change of sediment concentration (−3%~3%/year). For a consistent basis of comparison, we initialized the model with a wider profile for tidal flats with higher sediment availability, maintaining uniform parameters across all scenarios except for the initial SSC level and the SSC variation rates. For a given SSC level, we first obtained the equilibrium profile from the initial linear profile after 100 years of simulation, after which the change in the tidal flat morphology is negligible76. Based on the obtained equilibrium profile, we simulated the tidal flat morphological variations with changing SSC over 13 years (2003 to 2015, as a reflection of the observation), and finally compared the simulated flat width changes resulting from various SSC changing rates.

To test the observed elastic response of tidal flat morphology in China, we further analyzed the data from three other countries with substantial tidal flat areas, i.e., Indonesia, Australia, and the United States. There are a large number of observation transects in these countries and many of them are affected by direct human intervention. To select the representative transects, we categorized tidal flat transects from these three countries into four groups for each country, based on initial SSC levels (0-20 mg/L and >20 mg/L) and SSC change rates (-9 to -3%/year and 3 to 9%/year). Within each group, we randomly selected 50 tidal flat transects, and subsequently excluded the transects with direct human impact based on the satellite base map from Google Earth Engine. This resulted in 34 transects in Indonesia, 49 in Australia, and 33 in the USA. For China, we grouped SSC into sediment-starved and sediment-rich areas as mentioned in the previous section.

### Reviewer 2

In this manuscript the authors traced the spatial and temporal morphological changes of more than 2’500 tidal flat transects across China, unravelling the intricate controls governing their morphological evolution in response to changes in external forcing such as suspended sediment concentration (SSC), tidal range, and wave height. The objective of this study, of establishing a scientific foundation for informed management strategies is timely and relevant, considering the global decline of tidal flats in China and worldwide.
The authors demonstrate the correlations between tidal flat width and SSC distribution, as well as tidal flat slope and tidal range. Particularly noteworthy is the nationwide decrease in tidal flat width observed from 2002 to 2016 due to reduced SSC, underscoring the significant role of sediment supply dynamics. Furthermore, the authors' observation that sediment-rich tidal flats exhibit a swifter response to SSC reduction compared to sediment-poor tidal flats, and vice versa, highlights the nuanced interplay between sediment availability and tidal flat morphology. These responsive behaviors are underpinned by the capability of tidal flats to revert to their morphological equilibrium.
The research presented by the authors is well designed, scientifically sound, and is carried out in a consistent and rigorous way. I particularly appreciated the challenge of quantitatively unravelling the dependence of tidal flats from, and their response to, external forcing and changes thereof.
The huge dataset considered by the authors was properly analyzed and the conclusions are well supported by the results of the analyses. In particular, the finding that "sediment-rich tidal flats respond faster to SSC reduction compared to sediment-starving areas, but the opposite is true if SSC rises" could have important implications to tidal-flat dynamics in the face of anthropogenic pressure, which may help advance further studies in the field of coastal morphodynamics.
The manuscript is well-written and effectively communicates the findings to the intended audience. While the study is robust, there are critical areas for improvement that would enhance the manuscript's clarity, completeness, and overall impact.
As detailed in the specific comments below, my suggestions aim to:
i) Describe the different responses to changes in SSC of sediment-rich and sediment-poor systems. While the analogy with spring dynamics is nice, it is essential to explain what morphodynamic mechanisms and feedbacks control such a response. Providing a detailed explanation grounded in morphodynamic principles would strengthen the scientific basis of the observed behaviors.
ii) Discuss the applicability of their results in diverse coastal systems, especially where sediment availability could be considerably scarcer than that along the Chinese coast. Given that 50mg/L would equate to a substantial sediment concentration for some severely sediment-starved systems globally, broadening the study's relevance is essential.
iii) Consider whether the inclusion of sea level rise (SLR) effects could potentially impact the outcomes of this study. Addressing the potential impacts of SLR on the study outcomes ensures the robustness of the study's conclusions under varying conditions.
iv) Reconcile apparently divergent findings related to concave-up and convex profiles, along with their underlying factors. This includes explaining how these factors might influence the results and ensuring consistency with previous findings.
Based on these points, there is a clear need for substantial revisions to improve the manuscript before it can be considered for publication in Nature Communications. The issues highlighted and the suggestions provided below are aimed at enhancing the manuscript’s clarity, completeness, and scientific rigor, thereby elevating an already strong study to a higher standard of excellence.
Detailed comments.

### Reviewer 3

The paper presents a data-driven analysis of tidal flat morphology from spatial datasets across China's coastline. The synthesis work utilizes various spatial datasets with disparate temporal and spatial resolutions to ascertain the effect of suspended sediment concentrations, tidal range, and wave height on tidal flat width and slope. The paper finds that SSC is a major factor in tidal flat width and recommends excess sediment be allocated to low-sediment coastal systems.
The noteworthy results include positive correlation of tidal flat width with suspended sediment concentrations and tidal range and the tidal slopes positive correlation with tidal range. The authors suggest a limited impact of additional sediment in sediment rich coastal regions.
The work does have some limitations. By ignoring the largest driver of loss i.e. direct conversion, the authors have limited the impact of the work. A brief discussion on anthropogenic loss would increase the impact of the work, as tidal flat ecosystems with partial conversion to aquaculture and other land uses are expected to have unique morphology and change trajectories. Additionally, the 917 transects with discontinuous elevation should be discussed further. Is this a FAST database issue or an indication of anthropogenic impacts?
Uncertainty and error are mentioned but need to be thoroughly discussed for each dataset. For example, tidal flat accuracy is 82.2%, and the FAST database has a vertical accuracy of 30-50 cm accuracy. No uncertainty is reported for the TPXO9-atlas atlas or the ERA-5. While error propagation would be ideal for these datasets, that is probably not feasible. However, discussing how these errors might affect the results is necessary.
Additionally, Figure 1 should not use error bars for quantile ranges; instead, a boxplot would be more appropriate as the current visualization suggests to a viewer that this is the error of the slope.
The various data transformations may appropriately handle autocorrelation, but the current paper ignores spatial autocorrelation entirely. An exploration of Moran's I is appropriate.

1.3 The second one is that is it appropriate to use SSC to characterize the sediment
supply as the authors ignored the dynamic factors, such as sea level rising, change of
tides and wind-waves, and terrigenous sediment supply? Also, even the tidal flat change
itself can drive SSC variation. So, how to analyze the nonlinear correlation between
them? In my opinion, both the methodology and the results of this manuscript are not
sound.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for these questions and realize that a better explanation is needed
on why we use SSC to characterize the sediment availability.
Firstly, indeed, the changes of tidal flat itself may lead to SSC variation, but such an
impact is considered small compared to human induced SSC variation (e.g. damming),
as indicated by studies on global-scale SSC in coastal areas (Dethier et al., 2022; Hou
et al., 2024). Correspondingly, our data also imply that the impact of tidal flat change
on SSC is small, as the overall SSC drops with a reduction in tidal flat width (Fig. 3c,
d). If tidal flat change would have a large impact on SSC, the reduction in tidal flat
width would lead to more sediment into the water column, and would mitigate the SSC
reduction. However, such mitigation is not observed from our dataset, which implies
the nonsignificant role of tidal flat width on SSC. Secondly, SSC is commonly
considered to be a key external driver of intertidal morphological changes in previous
studies (e.g., Fagherazzi et al., 2006; Friedrichs, 2011; Kirwan et al., 2010, 2016; Maan
et al., 2015; Roberts et al., 2000), in which the impact of tidal flat change on SSC is
rarely considered, and is beyond the scope of the current study.
Additionally, we agree that it is necessary to consider the potential impacts of variations
in wind waves, tidal range, and sea-level rise.
To quantify the possible importance of the change of waves, we newly calculated the
change rate of significant wave height at 105 sites along the coast of China (with a
resolution of 0.5 degrees) from ERA5 data. The results show that 95% of tidal flat areas
have experienced very limited wave height variability (below 0.1 cm/year) compared
to tidal flat area changes from 2002 to 2016. Therefore, for the considered period, there
is no significant correlation between the wave height change rate and the change rate
of tidal flat width on China’s coast (p = 0.42).
Regarding the change of tidal range, we calculated the change rates of tidal range from
TPXO9 data, but the results indicated no significant correlation between the changes in
tidal flat width and tidal range (p = 0.25). This may be due to the relatively small
changes in tidal range along China's tidal flats during the study period, with an
average change of 0.3% per year.
Regarding sea-level rise (SLR), we newly included additional data on SLR from 14
coastal stations in China, and did a correlation analysis between SLR and tidal flat width and
SLR. We found that there is no significant correlation between SLR and the local changes in
tidal flat width (p=0.89). This lack of correlation is likely due to the relatively short
time scale of interest.
To demonstrate the validity of considering SSC change as arepresentative driver for
tidal flat width change, we added text in lines 455-456 as:
“SSC is considered representative of the local sediment availability35–37,59, and a key
external driver on tidal flat morphodynamics.”
To indicate the impact of the wave, we included the text in lines 442-446 as:

1.11 Line 193: The sediment condition is defined by the SSC in the tidal flat. So, are
all the tidal flats in sediment-rich area higher than the morphological equilibrium
(convex) and those in sediment-starving area lower than the equilibrium (concave)?
Response:
We thank the reviewer for the comment. No, the tidal flats in sediment-rich areas are
not always higher than the morphological equilibrium and those in sediment-starved
areas are not always lower than the equilibrium either. According to the original
literature on dynamic equilibrium theory (Friedrichs, 2011) and later in the subsequent
review (Green & Coco, 2014), sediment-rich systems typically have a convex profile
as their morphological equilibrium, while sediment-starved systems often have a
concave profile. Thus, we followed these previous theoretical studies and used the
convex and concave profiles to represent sediment-rich and sediment-starved flats,
respectively.
To make the above point clear, we add text in the caption of Fig.4 in lines 224-226, as:
“The convex shape of sediment-rich flats and the concave shape of the sediment-starved
flats correspond to the ideal profiles from the dynamic equilibrium theory18,25.”
1.12 Line 255-256: It is curious what is the critical condition for tidal flat morphology
tending to move towards the equilibrium state rather than being driven away from it if
the initial morphology reached the equilibrium.
Response:
We included the following text in the Discussion (lines 301-312) to explain the
mechanism that tidal flat morphology tending to move towards the equilibrium state
rather than being driven away from it:
“The conditional responses of tidal flat morphology can be explained by the balance
between sediment availability and hydrodynamic forcing. Sediment-rich tidal flats
typically have flatter and shallower profiles, which are subject to greater wave and
current induced bed shear stresses9. On these flats, surplus sediment is less likely to
settle, hindering tidal flat expansion, but a sediment availability deficit can easily lead
to rapid erosion due to the primitive high level of bed shear stress. Conversely,
sediment-starved flats have relatively lower bed shear stresses due to the steeper and
deeper profiles9, making them able to accommodate surplus sediment and resistant to
further erosion during sediment deficit. These conditional responses lead to the
observed spring-like behaviors of tidal flat morphodynamics that tend to move towards
the equilibrium state rather than being driven further away from it (Fig. 4). This
mechanism can be well explained from a modeling perspective, provided in
Supplementary Text.”

areas subject to strong wave action.
However, to our knowledge, this tidal flat area map is the only freely accessible tidal
flat dataset that enables doing large-scale analysis such as needed for the current study.
Based on the accuracy of the original data (>80%), we believe that the inaccuracy in
the datasets is not so large that it would affect the main findings of the current study.
To elucidate the sources of possible errors, we have added text in lines 368-374:
“The overall accuracy of the tidal flat area map is 82.2%39. Misclassification of tidal
flats (pixels) can occur in areas of highly turbid water, polluted areas, aquaculture
ponds, and areas subject to strong wave action. Despite the potential errors, to our
knowledge, this map is the only freely accessible tidal flat map that covers large spatial
(national) and temporal (decadal) scales. The accuracy of this map is sufficient
(>80%)39 to reveal the overall dynamics of tidal flat areas and to support the main
findings of the current study.”

Reviewer #1 (Remarks on code availability):
There is no README file with enough instructions for installing and running the

Response:
We thank the reviewer for the reminder. We have added a README file with

2. Response to Reviewer #2 (in blue):
2.1 In this manuscript the authors traced the spatial and temporal morphological
changes of more than 2’500 tidal flat transects across China, unravelling the intricate
controls governing their morphological evolution in response to changes in external
forcing such as suspended sediment concentration (SSC), tidal range, and wave height.
The objective of this study, of establishing a scientific foundation for informed
management strategies is timely and relevant, considering the global decline of tidal
flats in China and worldwide.
The authors demonstrate the correlations between tidal flat width and SSC distribution,
as well as tidal flat slope and tidal range. Particularly noteworthy is the nationwide
decrease in tidal flat width observed from 2002 to 2016 due to reduced SSC,
underscoring the significant role of sediment supply dynamics. Furthermore, the
authors' observation that sediment-rich tidal flats exhibit a swifter response to SSC
reduction compared to sediment-poor tidal flats, and vice versa, highlights the nuanced
interplay between sediment availability and tidal flat morphology. These responsive
behaviors are underpinned by the capability of tidal flats to revert to their morphological
equilibrium.
The research presented by the authors is well designed, scientifically sound, and is
carried out in a consistent and rigorous way. I particularly appreciated the challenge of
quantitatively unravelling the dependence of tidal flats from, and their response to,
external forcing and changes thereof.
The huge dataset considered by the authors was properly analyzed and the conclusions
are well supported by the results of the analyses. In particular, the finding that
"sediment-rich tidal flats respond faster to SSC reduction compared to sediment-
starving areas, but the opposite is true if SSC rises" could have important implications
to tidal-flat dynamics in the face of anthropogenic pressure, which may help advance
further studies in the field of coastal morphodynamics.
The manuscript is well-written and effectively communicates the findings to the
intended audience. While the study is robust, there are critical areas for improvement
that would enhance the manuscript's clarity, completeness, and overall impact.
Response:
We are very grateful for the reviewer’s positive evaluation of our paper, and for
recognizing it being timely and relevant for management. Below, we provide a point-
by-point response to the reviewer’s comments and show how they are incorporated into
the revised manuscript.
2.2 i) Describe the different responses to changes in SSC of sediment-rich and
sediment-poor systems. While the analogy with spring dynamics is nice, it is essential
to explain what morphodynamic mechanisms and feedbacks control such a response.
Providing a detailed explanation grounded in morphodynamic principles would
strengthen the scientific basis of the observed behaviors.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this comment. Indeed, it is essential to explain what
morphodynamic mechanisms and feedback control such a response. Thus, we revised
lines 301-312 in the main text for a concise explanation, which illustrates the
mechanism of the spring-like change of tidal flat width to SSC from a modeling
perspective.
“The conditional responses of tidal flat morphology can be explained by the balance
between sediment availability and hydrodynamic forcing. Sediment-rich tidal flats
typically have flatter and shallower profiles, which are subject to greater wave and
current induced bed shear stresses9. On these flats, surplus sediment is less likely to
settle, hindering tidal flat expansion, but a sediment availability deficit can easily lead
to rapid erosion due to the primitive high level of bed shear stress. Conversely,
sediment-starved flats have relatively lower bed shear stresses due to the steeper and
deeper profiles9, making them able to accommodate surplus sediment and resistant to
further erosion during sediment deficit. These conditional responses lead to the
observed spring-like behaviors of tidal flat morphodynamics that tend to move towards
the equilibrium state rather than being driven further away from it (Fig. 4). This
mechanism can be well explained from a modeling perspective, provided in
Supplementary Text.”
Additionally, we also rewrite the supplementary section (Supplementary Fig. 19 and
Supplementary Text) to explain the mechanism from a modeling perspective.
2.3 ii) Discuss the applicability of their results in diverse coastal systems, especially
where sediment availability could be considerably scarcer than that along the Chinese
coast. Given that 50mg/L would equate to a substantial sediment concentration for some
severely sediment-starved systems globally, broadening the study's relevance is
essential.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for the suggestion. In the revised manuscript, our theory has
been confirmed in countries with lower sediment availability, including Indonesia,
Australia, and the United States, three countries with extensive tidal flat areas (ranked
1st, 3rd, and 4th globally). The relevant results are included in the new Fig. 5 in the
revised manuscript.
[panel redacted]
Fig. 5 – Modeled and observed tidal flat width response to sediment availability
changes. (a) The contour map represents the tidal flat width change corresponding to
different variation rates in SSC from DET-ESTMORF modeling, whereas bubbles
indicate the representative data points for tidal flat width changes and the number
indicates the location along China’s coast (see methods for data selection). Red bubbles
indicate tidal flats expansions, and green bubbles indicate tidal flat retreats. The size
of the bubbles indicates the variation rate. The upper left and lower right corners of the
diagram are two ‘hot’ zones, i.e., sediment-starved sites with an increase of SSC and
sediment-rich sites with SSC drop. The area between the two solid black lines indicates
a ‘neutral’ zone where the interannual variation of tidal flat widths is within -0.1% and
0.3%. There are no data points in the upper left corner, i.e., rapid SSC increase (> 1%
per year) in sediment-rich systems. (b) The rate of tidal flat width changes in relation
to the initial SSC level when SSC increases by 3 ~ 9 %/year in all four countries (p <
0.01), indicating slower expansion of sediment-rich areas if SSC increases. (c) The rate
of tidal flat width changes in relation to the initial SSC level when sediment decreases
by 3 ~ 9 %/year in the four countries (p < 0.05), indicating faster retreat of sediment-
rich areas if SSC decreases. The brown line is the linear regression line with the p-
value. Data from these countries are randomly selected based on their initial SSC level
and SSC change rate (see Methods). ‘N’ means the number of data points selected from
each country.
To illustrate the methodology for selecting representative points, we added text in lines
617-627 as:
“To test the observed elastic response of tidal flat morphology in China, we further
analyzed the data from three other countries with substantial tidal flat areas, i.e.,
Indonesia, Australia, and the United States. There are a large number of observation
transects in these countries and many of them are affected by direct human intervention.
To select the representative transects, we categorized tidal flat transects from these
three countries into four groups for each country, based on initial SSC levels (0-20 mg/L
and > 20 mg/L) and SSC change rates (-9 to -3 %/year and 3 to 9 %/year). Within each
group, we randomly selected 50 tidal flat transects, and subsequently excluded the
transects with direct human impact based on the “satellite” base map from Google
Earth Engine. This resulted in 34 transects in Indonesia, 49 in Australia, and 33 in the
USA. For China, we grouped SSC into sediment-starved and sediment-rich areas as
mentioned in the section “Suspended Sediment Concentration (SSC) data”.”
To discuss the applicability of the theory in other countries, we revised the text in lines
479-481 and 255-261 as:
“These thresholds can be considerably higher than other countries15,65, due to the
overall higher SSC on China’s coast. Thus, sediment-starved and sediment-rich systems
should be defined differently in other regions of the world.”
“The observed elastic response of tidal flat morphology in China also has global
relevance, as similar dynamics are observed from three other countries with substantial
tidal flat areas, i.e., Indonesia, Australia, and the United States. These three countries
are ranked 1st, 3rd, and 4th place globally in tidal flat areas (with China being the 2nd
place). Data from these four countries collectively show: 1) tidal flat width grows if
SSC increases and shrinks if SSC declines; 2) tidal flats with higher SSC have lower
expansion rates as SSC increases, but higher retreat rates if SSC reduces (Fig. 5b, c).”
2.4 iii) Consider whether the inclusion of sea level rise (SLR) effects could potentially
impact the outcomes of this study. Addressing the potential impacts of SLR on the study
outcomes ensures the robustness of the study's conclusions under varying conditions.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for the comment. The supplementary data indicate that there is
no significant correlation between the changes in tidal flat width and SLR during the
study period.
We fully understand the reviewer’s concern on the impact of historical sea-level rise
and have included relevant discussion and references in the manuscript in Lines 342-
346 as:
“Due to the decadal time scale (2002-2016), sea-level rise does not have a clear impact
on tidal flat morphology based on data from 14 Chinese long-term water level
observation sites (p = 0.89, see Methods). However, over longer time scales (e.g., a
century), its impact can be pronounced, especially with concurrent SSC reduction22,35–
37, emphasizing the need to expand long-term monitoring in the future.”
Lastly, the reviewer also mentioned in comment 2.26 that he/she agrees that due to the
short time scale of the current study (14 years), it is acceptable not to consider sea level
rise as a factor.
2.5 iv) Reconcile apparently divergent findings related to concave-up and convex
profiles, along with their underlying factors. This includes explaining how these factors
might influence the results and ensuring consistency with previous findings.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for the comment. From the original literature on dynamic
equilibrium theory (Friedrichs, 2011), indeed sediment-rich systems often have convex
profile shapes while sediment-starved systems often have concave shapes. Thus, we
depicted the concave versus convex tidal flat profiles to correspond with sediment-
starved and sediment-rich systems in Fig 4. To make the above point clear, we added
the text in the caption of Figure 4 as:
“The convex shape of sediment-rich flats and the concave shape of the sediment-starved
flats correspond to the ideal profiles from the dynamic equilibrium theory18,25.”
2.6 Based on these points, there is a clear need for substantial revisions to improve the
manuscript before it can be considered for publication in Nature Communications. The
issues highlighted and the suggestions provided below are aimed at enhancing the
manuscript’s clarity, completeness, and scientific rigor, thereby elevating an already
strong study to a higher standard of excellence.
Response:
We appreciate the reviewer’s kind evaluation of our work as an ‘already strong study’
and the constructive suggestions. Detailed responses are listed below.
Detailed comments.
2.7 Line 42. Noun as adjective. Change “tidal flats dynamics” to “tidal flat dynamics”.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this comment. The text has been revised.
2.8 Line 46. Do you refer to worldwide decline?
Response:
Here we refer to the loss of tidal flat areas worldwide. The text has been revised in line
43 as:
“Strikingly, approximately 16% of the global tidal flat area was lost during 1984-2016”
2.9 Lines 47-90. In the Introduction, the authors miss to include important literature in
the introduction that could provide additional context and support for their findings.
Indeed, it would be worth mentioning that researchers in the field have demonstrated
through both point (Fagherazzi et al., PNAS 2006; Marani et al., JGR-ES, 2010) and
spatially explicit (Roberts et al., CSR 2000; Hu et al., JGR-ES 2015) models and
analyses, that tidal flats can attain a dynamic equilibrium condition influenced by the
external forcing considered by the authors. This suggestion is rooted in the authors'
application of the equilibrium theory to support their findings and subsequent
interpretations within the text.
Response:
We agree with the reviewer that it is important to provide a context of dynamic
equilibrium theory for the subsequent application of the theory. Thus, we included the
suggested references in lines 79-80 in the new paper as:
“Finally, the observed diverse morphological responses were explained by a model
based on dynamic equilibrium theory9,10,18,20–22.”
2.10 Lines 67-70. These lines are unclear. Although the authors refer readers to the
Methods section, there remains uncertainty about the meaning of "independent and
complete profiles" and "elevation continuous profiles."
Response:
The text has been revised in lines 69-72 and 383-386 as:
“These transects are selected at 1 km resolution, covering open-coast and estuaries,
but those affected by direct human impact or where the width or slope information
cannot be extracted were excluded from the analysis (see Methods).”
“Transects with discontinuous elevation were excluded from analysis (917 of 2538
transects). There are mainly two reasons that cause the discontinuous elevation: 1) gaps
within the continuous elevation data (51.4%); 2) none or too few elevation data in the
FAST database (48.6%).”
2.11 Line 86. There is an extra period in the sentence.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for the comment. The text has been revised accordingly.
2.12 Lines 87-88 and 102-107. The authors state that the average width of tidal flats in
estuaries is greater than that of flats on open coasts, likely due to sediment availability.
However, they do not provide sufficient evidence to support this claim. Additionally,
regarding tidal flat slope (lines 102-107), it is unclear what factors determine the
difference between Fujian and Jiangsu.
Response:
We calculated the average SSC for both estuarine and open coastal areas of tidal flats.
The SSC in estuaries is significantly higher than that on the open coast (74.0 mg/L vs.
47.4 mg/L), which may serve as supporting evidence. Additionally, the high slope of
tidal flats in Fujian is a characteristic of its relatively large mean tidal range of 3.6 m
and low SSC level of 29 mg/L, whereas the lower slope of tidal flats in Jiangsu is
influenced by high SSC (110.0 mg/L) and the moderately high tidal range (2.93 m).
To make this point clear, we revised the text in lines 89-95 and 111-115 as follows:
“To compare the tidal flats in estuaries and on open coasts, we selected 5 major
estuaries in China, namely the Changjiang River Estuary, the Yellow River Estuary, the
Pearl River Estuary, the Minjiang River Estuary, and the Liaohe River Estuary
(Supplementary Fig. 2)23 for analysis. Notably, the median flat width in these estuaries
(807 m, N = 275) is greater than those on open coasts (512 m, N = 2263), which is
likely attributed to the higher median SSC for estuarine tidal flats (71.0 mg/L) than
their open coast counterparts (44.0 mg/L).”
“The tidal flats in southern Fujian have the highest median slope in the country, i.e.,
1.5×10-2 (Fig. 1b), which is influenced by the large tidal range (3.6 m) and a low SSC
level (29 mg/L). In contrast, those in southern Jiangsu show the lowest slope i.e.,
6.7×10-4, influenced by the exceptionally high SSC (110 mg/L) and a moderate tidal
range (2.93 m).”
2.13 Lines 109-116 and Figure 2. Frankly, I don't understand why the relationship
between Average Width and Wave Height, or between Slope and Wave Height, is not
shown. Given that the correlation between tidal flat slope and tidal range is weak (R^2
= 0.30), what would be the correlation between tidal flat slope and wave height?
Furthermore, why do the authors consider average width, while examining the median
slope?
Response:
We are grateful for the reviewer's comments and concur that it is necessary to include
a plot indicating the relationship between wave height and the width and slope in Figure
2. Additionally, we calculated the correlation coefficient between the tidal flat slope and
wave height to be 0.13 (p > 0.05), and the correlation coefficient between tidal range
and slope to be 0.34 (p < 0.01). The correlation coefficient for tidal flat width and wave
height is -0.20 (p < 0.05).
Additionally, considering the large distribution range of the tidal flat width (30-26000
m) and slope (3.6×10-5-1.2×10-1), we agree that it is better to consider the median value
for both width and slope, instead of the average width. To make these points clear, we
revised the lines in 120-122, 140-141 and Figure 2 as:
“The results show that tidal flat width exhibits a positive correlation with SSC (R =
0.71, P < 0.01) and tidal range (R = 0.44, P < 0.01) but a weaker negative correlation
with wave height (R = -0.20, P < 0.05, Fig. 2e).”
“Waves are known to have an impact on tidal flat slope9,18, but it is not significant in
the current dataset (R = 0.13, P > 0.05; Fig. 2f).”
Fig. 2 - Relations between the spatial distribution of tidal flat width and slope with SSC
(a, b), tidal range (c, d), and wave height (e, f). The number displayed at the base of
each bar represents the number of data points of tidal flat width (average of 2014-2016)
and slope (average of 1997-2017). (g, h) Linear regression models (solid lines) that
best explain the distribution of width and slope with 95% confidence intervals (shaded
areas), in which data are transformed to ensure normal distribution. The effect of
spatial autocorrelation is excluded through the application of a spatial error model
(details of data processing are included in Methods).
2.14 Lines 135-143. What about the effect of wave heights on both tidal flat width and
slope?
Response:
In our data analysis, tidal flat width is inversely correlated with wave height, with a
correlation coefficient of -0.20 that is statistically significant (P < 0.05). The tidal flat
slope correlates positively with wave height, but this correlation is not statistically
significant (R = 0.13, P > 0.05).
The mechanism is that higher waves would create higher peaks in bed shear stress
during wave breaking, which can easily erode the tidal flat profile, resulting in steeper
profile slopes and narrower widths. To make these points clear, we added the text in
lines 120-122 and 140-141 as:
“The results show that tidal flat width exhibits a positive correlation with SSC (R =
0.71, P < 0.01) and tidal range (R = 0.44, P < 0.01) but a weaker negative correlation
with wave height (R = -0.20, P < 0.05, Fig. 2e).”
“Waves are known to have an impact on tidal flat slope9,18, but it is not significant in
the current dataset (R = 0.13, P > 0.05; Fig. 2f).”
2.15 Lines 135-143. In certain microtidal systems like the Venice Lagoon (Italy) or the
Virginia Coast Reserve (USA), where wind waves exert greater influence than tidal
oscillations, tidal flats exhibit nearly negligible slopes (in fact, they are exceptionally
flat!), yet the shift from tidal flats to marshes occurs through an exceptionally steep
(almost vertical) scarp. How does this observation align with or challenge your findings?
Please comment.
Response:
Indeed, it is known from previous studies (Friedrichs, 2011; Roberts et al., 2000) that
tidal flats in micro-tidal systems have a very low slope. This is complementary to our
results as shown in Figure 2. In such cases, the effect of waves is more important. To
make this point clear, we added the following text in the Discussion section in lines
287-292 as:
“In this study, we use China’s tidal flat ecosystem as an example and elucidate that
tidal range predominantly influences the slope of tidal flats, compared to incident waves
or SSC. In our system, a higher tidal range typically leads to a steeper slope. This is
complementary to the observations from microtidal systems like the Venice Lagoon
(Italy) or the Virginia Coast Reserve (USA), where the tidal flats are exceptionally level
due to the low tidal ranges9,26.”
2.16 Lines 145-148. In both Figure 3 and previous figures, does it make sense to
consider the average width of tidal flats, which ranges from 30 to 26,000 meters?
Response:
We agree with the reviewer on this comment that considering the average width of the
tidal flats is not meaningful when there is a large variation in tidal flat widths.
Accordingly, we revised the figures to calculate the median width in Figures 1-3.
2.17 Lines 143-152. 28.3% of sites experienced expansion. What is the percentage of
sites which experienced erosion?
Response:
30.3% of the tidal flat sites showed an erosion trend > 1% per year. To make this point
clear, we added the text in line 163 as:
“30.3% of tidal flats experienced a width reduction rate greater than 1% per year.”
2.18 Line 174-189 Contrasting Sediment-Rich and Sediment-Starved Tidal Flats How
is the threshold defined? Is the threshold based on the annual mean of the monthly mean
Suspended Sediment Concentration (SSC) data? Could you kindly provide clearer
clarification of this aspect either within the main text or in the section titled “Suspended
Sediment Concentration (SSC) Data”?
I am curious about the 50mg/L and 75mg/L thresholds for sediment-starved tidal flats
on the open coast and on estuaries, respectively, and whether those threshold are
affected by the specific SSC values of the area. A mean value of 50mg/L does not strike
me as indicating low sediment availability. Moreover, the SSC on the Chinese coast, as
considered by the authors, might be considerably higher than that of many other coastal
systems globally. Has your detailed scrutiny of the literature identified such a threshold?
How does this value compare to thresholds observed in other sediment-starved systems
worldwide?
Response:
The threshold for sediment-starved systems is determined based on the multi-year
average suspended sediment concentration (SSC) on the tidal flats in China, including
both open coast and estuaries (50 mg/L), and we consider areas below the average to
be sediment-starved systems. The threshold for sediment-rich systems (75 mg/L) is
determined from the multi-year average SSC in estuaries with typically high sediment
availability.
Additionally, our theory has been confirmed in countries with lower sediment
availability, and the detailed responses for the global applicability are provided
collectively in comment #2.3.
To clarify the rationale behind the selection of the threshold, we revised the text in lines
190-195 as:
“Beyond the overall connection between SSC reduction and tidal flat width loss, we
further discover diverse responses of sediment-starved (SSC < 50 mg/L, average SSC
of China’s tidal flats) and sediment-rich (SSC > 75 mg/L, average SSC in five major
Chinese estuaries, Supplementary Fig. 2; the Changjiang River Estuary, the Yellow
River Estuary, the Pearl River Estuary, the Minjiang River Estuary, and the Liaohe
River Estuary) sites to altered sediment availability.”
To make clear that these values may be different in other areas, we also added the
following text in Lines 479-481 as:
“These thresholds can be considerably higher than other countries15,65, due to the
overall higher SSC on China’s coast. Thus, sediment-starved and sediment-rich systems
should be defined differently in other regions of the world.”
2.19 Lines 177-179. Regarding the SSC decrease, is it meaningful to highlight an
average difference of 0.03% between sediment-rich and sediment-starved systems?
Could such a small difference fall within the margin of error due to estimations in tidal-
flat width and/or SSC concentration values? Additionally, note that the 0.27% and 0.24%
rates refer to an SSC decrease between 1.2% and 4%, while for the 0-1.2% decrease
scenario, the results are different. A similar consideration applies to the increase in SSC.
Response:
We agree that an average difference of 0.03% may not be significant. Therefore, we
examined a wider range of SSC variations from 1.2% to 4.8%, at which point the
difference in tidal flat erosion between the sediment-rich and sediment-starved systems
is 0.17% (0.27% vs 0.10% per year). For cases where the SSC increases, we also
provide more detailed results, similarly.
Accordingly, we revised the text in lines 195-199 and Figure 4 as:
“Notably, sediment-rich sites undergo 2.7 times faster width reduction than sediment-
starved sites (0.27% vs. 0.10% width loss per year) when SSC decreases between -1.2%
to -4.8% per year (Fig. 4a). Conversely, sediment-starved systems exhibit 2.1 times
more rapid width expansion (0.64% vs. 0.30% width gain per year) when SSC increases
between 1.2% to 4.8% per year.”
Fig. 4 - Elastic response of tidal flats width changes to altered sediment availability.
Flat width changes with sediment concentration change in sediment-rich and sediment-
starved areas based on observation (a) and explanatory modeling (b). The numbers at
the base of each bar represent the number of observations. Model results are based on
an exemplified sediment-rich site and a sediment-starved site (see Methods). (c)
Diagram showing a sediment-rich tidal flat is similar to a stretched spring that tends
to return to its morphological equilibrium (dashed line) and is resistant to being
stretched further. (d) Diagram showing a sediment-starved tidal flat is similar to a
compressed spring that tends to restore its morphological equilibrium (dashed line) and
resists being compressed further. The convex shape of sediment-rich flats and the
concave shape of the sediment-starved flats correspond to the ideal profiles from the
dynamic equilibrium theory18,25.
2.20 Lines 174-190 and Figure 4. What I observe here is that as the SSC decreases, both
sediment-rich and sediment-starved tidal flats exhibit a similar response by narrowing
their width at the same rate when considering actual tidal flats (Fig. 4a). However,
model results suggest a more pronounced decrease in width for sediment-rich tidal flats.
In this case, the model appears to overestimate the reduction in the width of the tidal
flats. The opposite appears to happen when there is an increase in SSC. Could this
suggest that the model is highly responsive to changes in SSC?
Moreover, while for the observations, the reduction in width with decreasing SSC
occurs at the same rate for both sediment-starved and sediment-rich systems, and the
same applies to the increase in width with increasing SSC, this is not the case in the
model. Additionally, the model is practically insensitive to an SSC increase of 0.8%
for sediment-rich systems, whereas it is not for an increase to 2%.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for these questions. As our responses for comment #2.19,
sediment-rich and sediment-starved tidal flats exhibit significant differences in their
responses to changes in SSC.
In contrast to Fig. 4a, which contains data from many different sites, the model results
in Fig. 4b are from two tidal flats as two exemplified sites to show the observed general
pattern (Fig 4a) in the data can be reproduced and explained by modeling. Thus, it is
meant for a qualitative comparison and explanatory modeling test with the observed
pattern.
We have included this information in the revised manuscript in lines 201-206.
“To elucidate these observed divergent responses, we conducted explanatory
simulations of a sediment-rich and a sediment-starved tidal flat using the DET-
ESTMORF model (Fig. 4b and Supplementary Fig. 9). The modeling results show
similar qualitative conditional responses to sediment availability changes, but have
different response rates in width change compared to observations. The latter is likely
caused by the fact that the simulations are based on two exemplified sites while not
account for all the observed variations across the country.”
2.21 Lines 182-197. Can the authors better describe the difference between actual
concentration and equilibrium concentration and how they are related to SSC?
Response:
Due to length limitations, we think it is better to include this detailed explanation in the
supplementary section, where the difference between actual concentration and
equilibrium concentration and how their interplay results in the conditional response of
tidal flat morphology are included. In relation to this comment, the explanation of the
tidal flat conditional response has been addressed in response #2.2.
2.22 Lines 204-213. The authors describe the different responses of sediment-rich and
sediment-poor systems using an analogy with the dynamics of a spring. While the
analogy with spring dynamics is illustrative, it would be beneficial to explain these
responses in terms of morphodynamic processes and feedbacks. Specifically, what
morphodynamic mechanisms and feedbacks control such responses? How do factors
like tidal range, sediment transport, deposition rates, erosion, and hydrodynamics
interplay to produce these observed behaviors? Providing a detailed explanation
grounded in morphodynamic principles would strengthen the understanding of these
differential responses to changes in SSC between sediment-rich and sediment-poor
systems.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for the comment, which would improve our manuscript. We
added the morphodynamic explanations in lines 301-312, as addressed in detail in
comment #2.2 above.
2.23 Lines 215-230. First. Figures 4C and 4D depict concave-up versus convex tidal
flat profiles and shapes. The same authors have previously explored and effectively
elucidated (Hu et al., JGR-ES 2015) this difference (convex shape for tide-dominated
areas; concave shape for wave-dominated areas). However, I don't recall this shape
difference being previously linked to sediment availability. Interestingly, in the present
study, the focus is solely on sediment availability, with no consideration given to the
potential influence of tidal range and waves. Could the authors provide insights into
reconciling these divergent findings?
Response:
Our response regarding the relationship between profile concavity and sediment
availability are provided in comment #2.5.
As for our focus in this paper, we investigate the influence of tidal range and waves in
the spatial tidal flat morphology. However, we did not study their effect on temporal
changes, since temporal changes in tidal range and wave climate were small given the
relatively short time frame that we considered (2002-2016).
To indicate the impact of wave, we included the text in lines 442-446 as:
“To assess if a change in waves might affect tidal flat width, we calculated the change
rate of significant wave height at 105 sites along the coast of China (with a resolution
of 0.5 degrees) from ERA5 data. It shows that 95% of tidal flat areas have experienced
a minimal variation in significant wave height below 0.1 cm/year from 2002 to 2016.
Thus, there is no significant correlation between the wave height change and tidal flat
width dynamics (p = 0.42).”
To indicate the impact of tidal range change, we included the text in lines 414-417 as:
“We also calculated the change rates of tidal range from TPXO9 data between 2002
and 2016, but the results indicated no significant correlation between the tidal flat
width changes and tidal range changes (p = 0.25). This may be due to the relatively
small changes in tidal range along China's tidal flats during the study period, with an
average change of 0.3% per year.”
2.24 Lines 215-230. Second. I do have a question. How do you determine the point at
which new equilibrium conditions are reached? Can you quantify the timescale over
which tidal flats respond to alterations in external forcing? More specifically, can you
determine the time it takes for certain physical properties (like elevation, accretion rate,
or progradation rate) to reach a specified percentage of their equilibrium value
following a change in forcing? (e.g. D’Alpaos et al., JGR 2011)? This could be quite
relevant as it would enable the estimation of the time needed for morphodynamic
equilibrium conditions to be attained (referred to as relaxation time).
Response:
We can quantify the timescale of relaxation time by calculating the elevation rate. To
do this, we added explanatory modeling and calculated the time to reach a new
equilibrium (elevation rate <1 mm/year) under a 2% increase and decrease in sediment
availability. Our modeling results indicate that sediment-rich systems reach equilibrium

more rapidly as sediment levels decrease (12 years < 24 years), whereas sediment-
starved systems reach equilibrium more quickly when sediment levels increase (19
years < 26 years). This result also confirms the phenomenon that sediment-rich systems
are more sensitive to sediment decrease. To make this point clear, we added the text in
lines 206-212 and Supplementary Figure 10:
“Following a previous study24, we further assess the relaxation time needed for new
stable profiles. When external sediment availability decreases by 2%, the sediment-rich
tidal flat reaches a new stable profile more quickly (12 years) than the sediment-starved
tidal flat (24 years). However, when sediment availability increases by 2%, the
sediment-starved tidal flat reaches a stable state more quickly (19 years) than the
sediment-rich site (26 years) (Supplementary Fig. 10). These results of relaxation time
are also clearly in line with the observed pattern of tidal flat width changes.”
Supplementary Figure 10. Modeled spatial-average elevation change rate of Jiangsu
and Western Scheldt tidal flat profile under a 2% decrease (a) and increase (b) in
sediment availability. Equilibrium points (the period when tidal flat morphological
equilibrium is reached) are defined as the spatial-average elevation change rate below
0.1 mm/year.
2.25 Lines 253-278. The authors did not demonstrate the possibility of extending their
results to other coastal systems worldwide. The considered case is quite particular
because, even in the case of sediment-poor systems, these systems are characterized by
SSC values much larger than those found in other coastal systems globally. Moreover,
there is a consensus that both sea level rise rates and sediment supply critically
influence coastal dynamics, determining their persistence or disappearance (e.g.,
Kirwan et al., GRL 2010; Marani et al., JGR-ES 2010; Kirwan et al., Nat. Climate
Change 2016; Mariotti and Carr, WRR 2014). The interplay of these factors should not
be assessed in isolation. Curiously, the rates of sea level rise impacting the Chinese
coast are not addressed in this study. Could this potentially impact your results? Might
this also influence the anticipated response of your study sites as sea level rise
accelerates?
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this comment and the suggested references. We have added
the analysis of three other countries with extensive tidal flat areas, which show the same
pattern (Fig. 5b and 5c). The responses for the global applicability are provided
collectively in comments #1.2 and #2.3.
As our response for the comment #2.4, there is no significant correlation between the
changes in tidal flat width and SLR during the study period. We fully understand
reviewer’s concern about the impact of sea-level rise and have included relevant
discussion and references in the manuscript in lines 342-346 as:
“Due to the decadal time scale (2002-2016), sea-level rise does not have a clear impact
on tidal flat morphology based on data from 14 Chinese long-term water level
observation sites (p = 0.89, see Methods). However, over longer time scales (e.g., a
century), its impact can be pronounced, especially with concurrent SSC reduction22,35–
37, emphasizing the need to expand long-term monitoring in the future.”
2.26 Lines 271-278 The authors mention that “due to the time scale (2002-2016) we
considered in the current study we did not include the impact of sea level rise, but over
several decades to centuries, its impact can be pronounced3”. I comprehend and concur
with this perspective. Nonetheless, if we aim to furnish long-term predictions,
accounting for SLR becomes imperative. How might the authors reassure readers that
these findings remain unaffected by varying SLR rates?
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this comment, and our responses are provided collectively in
comment #2.4 and #2.25.
3. Response to Reviewer #3 (in blue):
The paper presents a data-driven analysis of tidal flat morphology from spatial datasets
across China's coastline. The synthesis work utilizes various spatial datasets with
disparate temporal and spatial resolutions to ascertain the effect of suspended sediment
concentrations, tidal range, and wave height on tidal flat width and slope. The paper
finds that SSC is a major factor in tidal flat width and recommends excess sediment be
allocated to low-sediment coastal systems.
The noteworthy results include positive correlation of tidal flat width with suspended
sediment concentrations and tidal range and the tidal slopes positive correlation with
tidal range. The authors suggest a limited impact of additional sediment in sediment
rich coastal regions.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for the insightful summary of our paper. Below, we provide a
point-by-point response to the reviewer’s comments and show how they are
incorporated to improve the revised paper.
The work does have some limitations.
3.1 By ignoring the largest driver of loss i.e. direct conversion, the authors have limited
the impact of the work. A brief discussion on anthropogenic loss would increase the
impact of the work, as tidal flat ecosystems with partial conversion to aquaculture and
other land uses are expected to have unique morphology and change trajectories.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for the insightful suggestions. Regarding the direct effect of
human induced tidal flat loss, we excluded tidal flat transects directly affected by human
activities (e.g., conversion to other land use), which account for 26% of our dataset.
Additionally, the effect of damming is considered via the reduction of SSC at the coasts,
which is considered as a key environmental change on tidal flat morphology in the
current study. To make the above points clear, we added a discussion on human impact
in lines 331-335 and added Supplementary Figure 12 as:
“In our analysis, we focus on understanding how tidal flats respond to indirect external
disturbances from a morphodynamic perspective, while losses due to direct human
interventions (reclamation) are generally less predictable. Thus, we excluded data
points directly impacted by human activities, such as conversion to other land uses,
accounting for 26% of the total transects in our study (Supplementary Fig. 12).”
[figure redacted]
Supplementary Figure 12. Examples of tidal flat sites directly affected by human
activities. The red areas indicate the regions of tidal flats that have disappeared from
2002 to 2016 due to reclamation.
3.2 Additionally, the 917 transects with discontinuous elevation should be discussed
further. Is this a FAST database issue or an indication of anthropogenic impacts?
Response:
To provide the cause of the discontinuity, we added the text in lines 383-386 as:
“Transects with discontinuous elevation were excluded from analysis (917 of 2538
transects). There are mainly two reasons that cause the discontinuous elevation: 1) gaps
within the continuous elevation data (51.4%); 2) none or too few elevation data in the
FAST database (48.6%).”
3.3 Uncertainty and error are mentioned but need to be thoroughly discussed for each
dataset. For example, tidal flat accuracy is 82.2%, and the FAST database has a vertical
accuracy of 30-50 cm accuracy. No uncertainty is reported for the TPXO9-atlas atlas or
the ERA-5. While error propagation would be ideal for these datasets, that is probably
not feasible. However, discussing how these errors might affect the results is necessary.
Response:
In the revised manuscript, we clarify the errors in each database and their possible
impact on the results.
To explain the accuracy of the ERA-5 and TPXO9-atlas datasets, we include lines 424-
426 and 399-401 as:
“The database has been proven suitable for China's coastal areas48, with data bias
estimated at less than 0.1 m in deep waters.”
“The accuracy of the TPXO9 on China’s coast can be shown by an average Root Sum
Squares (RSS) value of 19.92 cm41.”
To discuss the influence of these errors on the results, we include the text in lines 335-
338 and 340-342 as:
“Additionally, cumulative errors from various data sources (e.g., FAST, ERA-5, tidal
flat map) in large-scale spatiotemporal studies could influence the accuracy of the
findings. For example, the tidal flat map data may misidentify highly turbid waters1,
which may lead to an overestimation of the tidal flat widths.”
“Despite these potential errors, our analysis aligns with dynamic equilibrium modeling
and is consistent with numerous previous studies9,10,18.”
3.4 Additionally, Figure 1 should not use error bars for quantile ranges; instead, a
boxplot would be more appropriate as the current visualization suggests to a viewer that
this is the error of the slope.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this kind comment. We have changed Figure 1 to show the
error of the slope as follows:
[panels redacted]
Fig. 1 - Distribution of tidal flats width (a) and slope (b) along the coast of China.
Coastal provinces of China are listed in the maps, namely Liaoning (LN), Hebei (HB),
